speechtext: May I address a question to the Minister of Finance and ask him if his attention has been drawn to a warning issued by Mr. Louis Rasminsky, governor of the Bank of Canada, in which he says that it would be dangerous to ignore the warning signals of rising prices and increasing costs. speechtext:

Last week the hon. member inquired about the valuation for duty being applied to imports of textiles from mainland China, and asked whether the valuation for duty applied to Hong Kong might be used instead of the one applied to Japan.
My colleague the Minister of National Revenue has informed me that imports from mainland China, of a class or kind made in Canada, are being valued for duty on the same basis as similar Japanese goods or their equivalent. Mr. Chairman, last evening at ten o'clock I was indicating that over the period of time that NATO has been in existence there has developed outside of NATO itself trading blocs reflecting the understanding that nations in Europe in particular have

DEBATES	February 8, 1966
concerning their self-preservation, namely, that they can best accomplish stability and growth in their economies by way of entering into trading relationships with other nations. As a result we have seen the development of the European Common Market, the European Free Trade Association and lately the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. This was one of the concepts envisaged for NATO on its formation in 1949 but it was one which was never permitted to develop within NATO because of powerful voices in NATO, notably that of the United States, which insisted that it remain purely a military organization and military machine.
So far as Canada is concerned, we have remained aloof from this growing economic relationship between countries. We have maintained our attachment to NATO only in the military sense and have not had any significant relationships with the trading blocs which have developed with the exception, of course, of being a member of the Commonwealth which dates back some years. I doubt very much that Canada's continued participation in NATO beyond the 20 year period will bring any measurable benefit to Canada itself. Because of the declining importance of maintaining a military machine in western Europe I doubt very much that Canada's continued participation in NATO will be of any great value to western Europe.
It seems to me, inasmuch as the expiration of the NATO agreement is approaching that Canada should be considering what its role should be in regard to NATO, and it also seems to me that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should give his opinion to the committee at this time as to just what Canada hopes to do when the 20 year period of NATO's existence rolls around in the spring of 1969. True, that is some three years or more away but that is not too long a period of time to start planning for our relationship with an organization such as NATO.
These are purely my own opinions, but inasmuch as there has been a complete failure because of lack of forcefulness on the part of certain nations in NATO, Canada being one of them, to develop within the NATO structure any form of economic alliance which would establish a stronger bulwark against intrusion by the Soviet bloc nations, it seems to me that our participation in NATO has come to an end and that it would serve no useful purpose to continue it beyond 1969.

I would seriously recommend that the government think in terms of withdrawing from NATO at that time and for the reasons I have outlined, namely: First, there has been a complete failure to develop within NATO any sort of economic interrelationships between the member countries. Second, this is the strongest bulwark which can be developed against intrusion by the Soviet bloc. Third, we are serving no great purpose for ourselves or for western Europe in remaining in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
NORAD is an entirely different sort of international relationship. The term of the agreement will expire some time in the spring of 1968, just two years hence. Likewise, I think that the government of Canada has a responsibility here first of all to outline to the house and to Canada what its feelings are with respect to continued participation in NORAD and, second, to take whatever steps it can to obtain the particular end which it has in view.
Again, for my part I think we are serving no valid function within the NORAD structure except to place our armed forces under the authority and dictation of another nation, the United States, which is the other party to NORAD. There are no pretensions about NORAD; it is purely a military structure. There were no thoughts in any way about its activating itself in any economic or social manner; it has a purely military structure. Its effect is to place Canadian troops under the control of United States military personnel and under the control and authority of the United States government should that government decide it is necessary to bring into play the military forces of the strategic air command and other sections of the United States national defence structure.
I would say that nearly all of the parties in Canada, some to a greater extent than others, have periodically over the years sought to advance the concept of participating in an international military sense only through the United Nations. We sought to advance the concept of a so-called world police force to assist in dampening altercations which arise between nations, to assist in preventing difficulties between nations from developing into global war, and to attempt to expand our concept of law enforcement within the nation to a world concept. I know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has this concept in mind and certainly his predecessor, Mr. Green, also had it in mind. Many attempts have been made in the United Nations to

speechtext:
The meeting which has been taking place in the past tew days in Honolulu between President Johnson of the United States and Prime Minister General Ky of South Viet Nam and the statements which have emanated from that meeting have been far from reassuring. I do not think anyone can read the reports published so far without feeling we have entered a stage where a further escalation of military activity in Viet Nam is likely. I wish to urge the government again to make the strongest possible protest against military escalation at this time because I believe that in the not too distant future, the United States will have passed beyond the point of no return.
It is often said the great danger is that the United States will come into confrontation with China. This, of course, is a real danger. Some of her best military experts in days gone by have warned the United States against becoming embroiled in a land war in Asia.
But there is another danger which has not been so readily recognized. This is the danger of a confrontation with the Soviet Union. Recently, Mr. Shelepin, the Soviet representative in Hanoi, announced publicly that the U.S.S.R. would honour its commitment to North Viet Nam in the event that Hanoi, Haiphong and the industrial areas of that country were bombed. The great danger as I see it is that if as a result of the negotiations now going on in Honolulu the United States decides to escalate its bombing of North Viet Nam in the Haiphong and Hanoi areas this will leave the Soviet Union with only two alternatives. One would be to ignore the situation and be accused of deserting its friends. The result would certainly be a loss of face in Africa and Asia. The second would be to give active military assistance to North Viet Nam and this could bring the two nuclear giants into confrontation. If this were to happen we could be embarked on a period of homicidal madness which might well menace the survival of mankind.
I think we have to appeal to the United States to stop the bombing in North Viet Nam and be prepared to accept two conditions essential to any successful peace negotiations. The first is that we must be prepared to treat with the National Liberation Front which at the present time controls some 60 per cent of the area of South Viet Nam and over 50 per cent of the population. It will not be sufficient for the United States to say that the National Liberation Front can have some representation on the delegation from North Viet Nam.

[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
If the National Liberation Front speaks for a substantial section of the population of South Viet Nam, surely they will have to be included officially as representatives, not necessarily the sole representatives, of the people of South Viet Nam. This, it seems to me, is a prior condition to any successful negotiation, and one which the United States government has never yet explicitly spelled out.
The second condition is that the United States must be prepared to forgo its oft-repeated statement that any negotiations must result in an independent, sovereign state of South Viet Nam being established. That is in complete violation of the commitment contained in section 7 of the 1954 Geneva Accord to which the United States itself on July 21, 1954, gave unilateral concurrence. That agreement provided that the temporary military line of demarcation was to be provisional subject to a free vote to allow the Vietnamese themselves to decide whether or not the temporary boundary would become a firm boundary or whether the people of Viet Nam desired to have the North and South amalgamate into a single state. There can be no hope of any successful negotiations until the United States is prepared to return to the spirit of the Geneva Accord to allow the people of Viet Nam to decide for themselves whether or not they want South Viet Nam to remain as an independent state or whether they want to merge these two countries into the position they were in prior to 1954.
In his newspaper article last week Mr. Charles Lynch said that he had information to the effect that the United States embassy in Ottawa was seriously contemplating lodging a protest with the government over the speech made by the hon. member for York South a week ago today. I do not know whether or not Mr. Lynch's information is accurate. I hope it is not, but I want to say that our friends in the United States embassy should know that they are not located in South Viet Nam or in the Dominican Republic. They are located in a free, independent, sovereign nation and we, the members of this House of Commons, reserve the right not only to criticize our own government but to criticize any other government or any policy, especially when we think that the future peace and security of the world is involved.

He talks about the rightwingers in our party, but sometimes when I listen to some members of his party it seems to me that they are more sympathetic to the viewpoint opposed to the west than otherwise.
You may ask, Mr. Chairman, why I make that statement and what is my premise. Prime Minister Wilson looked at some of his leftwingers one day, when they were taking the same position that has been taken by the leader of the New Democratic party, the hon. member for York South and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, and asked them whether they wanted the Communists to win. accompany war. There is not a member on either side of this house who does not sympathize in this regard, but surely we must be realistic.

They sent out feelers in an attempt to get both sides together to discuss and find a solution to the Viet Nam problem. They did this with the hope that the bombing would not be renewed and that the war there would not be extended throughout Asia. We all have this fear and hope that this will not occur.
I am sure the minister will agree with me when I say that the United States commenced a peaceful offensive at that time. Perhaps that term as used by newspapers and periodicals is not the term the President of the United States wanted used, because one wonders whether peace can be attained by an offensive action of any kind, but the fact is that the United States did, to use that term, inititate a peaceful offensive.
Following the action taken by the United States, did the rulers of Hanoi and the people of Peking get together? Did they attempt to do anything to discuss the problem in Viet Nam? Are the people of South Viet Nam and other parts of Asia going to succumb to Communism? One only has to remember the days when no one in Europe did anything about the Nazi threat. Hon. Ramsay Macdonald, at that time prime minister of Great Britain, Baldwin and many others peddled peace talk throughout Europe and the world just as salesmen sell life insurance, but eventually Naziism took over practically the whole of Europe. Great Britain and the Commonwealth stood alone during those years.
We must learn from the mistakes made by others in the past. Surely we are not going to make the same mistake in Asia as we made in Europe. I think we must admit that some of the examples we offer the rest of the world of the manner in which our society operates are not such as to cause other peoples without our traditions to decide that our ideas are the ones they wish to follow.
I merely remind you of some of the great sores in our so-called free enterprise system. There is the fact that even though you and I live in the second most wealthy country in the world, people who are not Communists tell us that 25 per cent of our people are living at or below the poverty line. Do you think that escapes the notice of people in the Communist half of the world? Do you think it escapes the notice of those people that we 
appear unable to cope with the corroding influences of delinquency in our society?
Do you think our society has been revealed to all of these people as the apogee of human achievement, that this is the best way in which people can organize themselves? Why should it? I again urge the members of the house, Mr. Chairman, to think very carefully before they too rashly endorse some of the policies that are now being pursued by the United States of America. I ask them to think before they endorse them in the face of the grave doubts and misgivings of some of the most responsible people in public life in the United States of America. Surely we arrogate to ourselves a greatly superior wisdom when we say we know better what is best for the world, best for the United States of America, that we know better than such people as those who have opposed in recent weeks and in recent months the policies of the administration of the United States. These are people who are day by day in contact with the actualities of that policy.
Does any member of this house take to himself the right to say he knows better than Senator Mansfield, better than Senator Wayne Morse, better than Senator Fulbright, better than one of the best informed columnists in the world, Mr. Walter Lippmann? Are they Communists? Perhaps they are. I do not believe even the members of the Conservative party would dare to call such people Communists. I suggest to them now is the time for a certain measure of humility on the part of Canadian citizens and Canadian members of parliament in the face of these ringing condemnations of the policy of the United States government, which our government so supinely supports and which the Conservative party vigorously and vociferously supports. I suggest this is an example of arrogance and ignorance which does no credit to the people of Canada.

Gardiner a question about butter and I received an eloquent and detailed answer on the subject of cheese. The principal objection of this party, which is apparent on reading the remarks made by various members including myself, is to the method employed by the government in its handling of the Rhodesian problem. We could go back about a year to the government's handling of another very important matter in Canada's foreign policy; I refer to the automobile pact with the United States. Here was a very important treaty affecting large segments of the economic life of Canada. This treaty was entered into by the government under authority which I think is a little more certain than the authority under which the Rhodesian proposals were introduced. Nevertheless we have not yet had an opportunity of dealing with the automobile pact in the house except during the question period and on one other brief occasion.
This was not the case in the United States. The pact was not ratified and put into effect until the United States congress had debated it and dealt with the matter. After all, it was this party which supported this idea in the first place. However, some of the terms in the pact are very unwise. If this pact had been brought before parliament for discussion and sent to a committee where the evidence of witnesses could have been heard, some of the problems now arising might have been avoided. For example, I understand that it has put out of commission quite a substantial business in the city of Galt, Ontario. But no, the government went right ahead without consulting anybody and without consulting parliament in particular.
Now we have the Rhodesian situation. As I pointed out in my earlier remarks, this has been a new and unique step which has been taken in Canadian foreign policy and in the methods by which we have applied our foreign policy. The matter was sufficiently important that parliament should have been called and given a White Paper on the facts. A great many members are satisfied with the facts on the one side, as some members of the New Democratic party apparently are. However, I have always found it wiser to ascertain the facts on both sides of a case. Had parliament been called the minister and the members of the cabinet could have had a consensus from the house. Mr. Chairman, I am intervening, prompted by two reasons. One is the interesting speech of the hon. lady from Vancouver-Kingsway whose presence in this house is welcomed because she is the daughter of a very distinguished and great Canadian. She was the wife of a very distinguished and great Canadian who was a Canadian of a particular quality in that he was a Prince Edward Islander. It is unlikely that I should agree with everything she says, but I admire her sincerity and her obvious conviction to the cause which she espouses. My other reason for saying a few words stems from what I hope is a misunderstanding on my part of some replies today and yesterday in reference to the initiative at the present time of the Holy Father, Pope Paul.
If I understood the suggestions or the implications, I am much surprised that anyone in the government believes that Canada properly is in a neutral category before the world. We are not an unaligned nation. We are non-belligerent, thank heaven, but Canada long since has made its commitment to one group in what has been for a long time a two power world.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Whether we like that continued status or not, it is generally the situation. We have for good reasons and, indeed, because of factors over which we have no control, found ourselves championing the cause of the leader of the so-called western bloc-the United States. Whether in one or two minutes I shall qualify for the category proposed by one of the members of the New Democratic party by being vigorous, vociferous, arrogant and ignorant, I do not know. But I should like to say for myself that I derive no satisfaction from any denigration of the United States for its actions in the face of such difficult problems as those arising in Viet Nam. Moreover, I doubt that this country benefits greatly from such denigration. The United States is one of the great functional democracies of the world. Every position taken within that country is open to public scrutiny and subject to public discussion and disagreement. Similarly we find that the allies who move with the United States constantly and as is their right discuss publicly the issues and goals they are trying to follow.
For the other side such a situation does not exist. I have heard of very few Voice of Women parades to Red Square. I have heard of few instances of tearing up draft cards in Peking. But the difficulty which constantly

presents itself to the makers of United States policy is that they must function at all times under the glare of public discussion and disagreement.
I think it is obvious to most Canadians that the security of Canada, our institutions and, to be old fashioned and perhaps trite, our way of life, depend on the continued success of the United States. We have seen on occasions in our own lifetime conflicts between great powers at explosive points. These were not resolved by declarations of intent or by mere expressions of good will. They had to be resolved by someone with sufficient strength of purpose and willingness to run a grave risk.
I would ask: What would the situation in Europe be today if the Truman doctrine had not been enunciated and acted upon in Greece and Turkey when the incursion of the Communists came there? What would have been the situation in the days of the Berlin airlift had not the western world, with the United States bearing the heaviest burden, declared and reiterated its intention to run through this blockade with an airlift even though it might be necessary to maintain it for 10, 20 or 50 years? What would have happened in Korea? Here was a reaffirmation of strength of purpose.
It is all very well to point out errors in United States strategy and tactics. Of course there are errors. But we must be mindful of the fact that it is the leaders and the people of the United States who are constantly bearing the burden. I wonder how many of those who criticize have looked at the tax bill the people of the United States are bearing.
I think one of the great fears of the western world is that the feeling might develop within the United States which was so prevalent there a generation ago, that they might accept the suggestion "Yanks go home" made by so many people. I should like to know what would happen if they did go home, if the people of the United States were to ask themselves, must we forever bear such a massive burden for such a large part of the world? I rejoice in nothing which might purposely or otherwise weaken the resolve of the American people to stand firm and to-stand strong.

I know some of the departmental information is classified. I believe they know more about these situations than I do, at least I hope they do, because half the information I get can only come from them. If they do not tell me everything then I cannot know all that they know, but I trust that with the knowledge they possess they will always have the ear of big brother, the United States, and will speak up bluntly and firmly.
I hope they will give the United States the benefit of the views of the small nations in exactly the same way as the Prime Minister did, when he took the views of the Canadian people and those of the then private member, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, to the United Nations and suggested the peace keeping force for which he, the Prime Minister, was personally praised, with Canada bathing in some of that reflected glory.
Canadians have always taken their part in international affairs and the only reason we cannot police the world is that we are not big enough. But I am sick and tired of being called a sheep merely because we have principles and freedoms of our own and are not willing to lie down before the red juggernaut and take our orders from Moscow. I do not think the members of the N.D.P. are Communists but with monotonous regularity they peddle the Communist line. This may well be due to ignorance, for which I feel sorry. They have my sympathy. But I am sick and tired of having it pounded into us that because we agree with the United States in her attempts to keep world peace we are neglecting the little people.
Where was the solidarity when we wanted to feed the hungry multitudes in China? There was no unanimity from that party then and I find it strange that they can change their ideas on international affairs day by day. They do not like the United States Monroe doctrine in relation to Cuba and they present the argument that we should espouse the Communist doctrine of non-interference in Asia.
If we did that we would never interfere in Cuba where the freedom of the little people is involved nor in Viet Nam where their freedom is also involved. I expect the Communists have as much right to interfere as we do but let us get our thinking straight about which side we support. You cannot keep holding on to the policeman's arm when he is trying to keep law and order. If he is not a good policeman, change him.
If we are not satisfied with the way the United States keeps the peace in southeast

Perhaps I may be a minority of one but I said before and I say again that if it is necessary to stem the red tide I am willing to join the United States forces as a private soldier and go and fight once more for the things in which I believe. That does not make me an American imperialist. It makes me a free Canadian citizen ready to fight for the things he believes in and ready to pay the price.
Was it United States interference in Cuba that caused all the trouble? When I first heard of Castro-I may say I am directing my remarks to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands-I thought that perhaps Castro was some kind of Cuban Robin Hood living in the hills and fighting for the little people, but when he and his men started shooting citizens in the street without a trial I began to think his orders were coming from the hammer and sickle because that is what was done in Russia in 1917 and what is done in every country the Communists seize. I repeat that I do not think the N.D.P. are Communists but I am getting very tired of them peddling the Communist line. If they are sincere about giving the little people of the world a chance, I suggest that once in a while they get behind the policeman and help bring about law and order.
Should atrocities be committed by American troops I would be the first to condemn them, but I am also ready to condemn atrocities committed by red troops, for example, the staking out of American soldiers and civilians. I shall not go into the details. The word "atrocity" puts a chill into anyone's heart. Wherever the Communist forces move we are supposed to back up and give ground. Why? Is it that we in Canada no longer believe in democracy? I think we do. I think all parties in this house do, but I give this warning: Do not be sucked in by the Communist line. Back up that policeman.
United Nations peace keeping forces have maintained peace in a number of areas of the world, notably the Gaza strip and Cyprus. The idea of peace keeping forces has worked. I should like to see these forces expanded many times until they are sufficient to maintain law and order everywhere. Then the United States could go home and provide its fair share of troops to the United Nations for peace keeping purposes.
Until this is done we have got to back up our great neighbour to the south. We have to

give all the encouragement we can to the effort to bring the nations of the world to the council table. We shall have to be willing to pay our fair share to provide adequate police forces so that people everywhere can have an opportunity to speak for those things in which they believe.

My hon. friend has asked me to reply to some specific questions. I had assumed that in the statement I made on Rhodesia the other night I dealt with all of the questions with the exception of the material which my hon. friend noted had been referred to by Mr. Menzies in another place.
The exchanges between Her Majesty's government in Britain and the regime of Mr. Smith are, of course, matters that involve those two authorities. The documents are all contained in the British Hansard and can readily be made available. I have already given instructions to ascertain whether loose copies of some of the particular documents, particularly the White Paper, can be obtained, and I will see that my hon. friend and other hon. members get these and that they will be available when the External Affairs Committee is sitting.
The problem involved here is that the British government had told the regime of Mr. Smith that it would be opposed to a unilateral declaration of independence. This declaration was threatened because of the insistence by the government of Britain that more progress be made in the removal of discriminations in Rhodesia. That was a matter which Rhodesia said was not the concern of the British government, and Rhodesia further said that if the British government insisted on the removal of these discriminations, or a phased program during which they would gradually be removed, then Mr. Smith would cause unilateral declaration of independence to be made and it is this unilateral declaration, this illegal act, this act of treason that is at issue and not the particular negotiations between the British government and the regime of Mr. Smith.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It is significant in this connection that we joined with the British government in opposing the illegal declaration because we be-
February 8, 1966

lieved Rhodesia should not become independent on the basis of the 1961 constitution without substantial modification. This was the issue. In theory this constitution could eventually produce majority rule, but this is something that Mr. Smith said would never occur in his lifetime. It was as a result of this refusal to recognize the desirability of giving better treatment to the majority of the people in the country, some three million of whom are black as opposed to some 400,000 who are white, that Mr. Smith was confronted, when he did make a unilateral declaration of independence, with the unanimous resistance of the Commonwealth.
As I said the other night, this resistance did not come as a surprise because long before the issue had been discussed formally at the Prime Ministers' Conference and the government of Rhodesia was informed what would happen in the event of such a declaration of independence. No one can suggest that we were going to oppose this unilateral declaration of independence solely because of the particular dispute between the British and the Rhodesian governments. We were opposed to a unilateral act of independence which was illegal and which had serious connotations for the unity of the Commonwealth.
My hon. friends have complained in their argument that the government resorted to procedures that were not in keeping with our parliamentary traditions, that we should have brought this matter first to the House of Commons I have dealt with that question. I may not have convinced my hon. friends but I dealt with it.
I indicated that our action in support of the position taken by the British government-the first action to be taken in support-seemed to us, as it seemed to others, necessary. There would have been no time for us to go through the procedures of calling parliament. The course that we followed was not a unique course. The Australian parliament happened to be in session, ours was not.

My hon. friend was generous enough in his remarks, I think of last night, to observe that the technicalities of the act, with which he is familiar because of the fact he was minister of trade and commerce at one time, had been observed.
We resorted to a complete and total embargo because we believed that this was a desirable and indeed the only act that we could take if a development in Commonwealth relations that would have been very serious was to be avoided.
My hon. friend asks, if the economic sanctions do not work, what then? In the first place I must tell him that it is the view of a number of governments, including the British government, that the sanctions will work, that these economic sanctions will have the intended result. I am not going to say that there can be no doubt about this. In these matters no human judgment can be certain or final, but it is our judgment that they will work. I am not suggesting that the sanctions that Canada by itself has imposed would have that result. We are not a participant in the oil sanctions, even though we have an oil embargo, for the simple reason that we do not export oil to Rhodesia, but the steps we have taken together with those of the British government, of the United States government, of the Scandinavian governments and the partial acts of certain countries like France, should have the results that I have indicated it is anticipated will follow.
My hon. friend asked why we removed our trade commissioner. We removed our trade commissioner because we wanted, by that preliminary act, to indicate our displeasure and concern about the act of this illegal administration. We were not the only country to do that. The British acted likewise even though the governor, the real authority in Rhodesia, continues to function as the legal embodiment of power. Other countries withdrew their representatives. We kept our assistant trade commissioner there for a few weeks after the withdrawal of the trade commissioner. I am sure that the course we have taken is the correct one. I can tell my hon. friend that it has not in any way denied us an opportunity of making an accurate assessment of the situation.

The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquar-rie) said a few moments ago that he hoped that in the reply the Prime Minister made today
February 8, 1966

in answer to a question put by the right hon. gentleman he was not suggesting that Canada occupied a neutral position. Of course Canada is not a neutral power. Canada is a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, an organization in which, I would say in answer to the hon. member for Skeena, Canada continues to believe as necessary for our security. We propose to maintain our membership in NATO for reasons that are no less important than those which brought about the establishment of NATO. So we are not a neutral nation.
That question was not involved in the reply given by the Prime Minister. The question was whether Canada had given any support to the proposal made to the United Nations by His Holiness Pope Paul VI. The Prime Minister noted that I had made known yesterday the view of the Canadian government that this was an appeal that should be supported, and to the extent that Canada is able to contribute by giving its support this will be done. The appeal addressed to the neutral powers was to the effect that they set up arbitration machinery to assist in ending the conflict in Viet Nam. The United States government itself incorporated in the resolution placed by Mr. Goldberg before the Security Council an acceptance of this proposal by the Pope.
Not only has this appeal been made by the Pope, whose memorable statement to the United Nations on October 6 has served to provide very important guide lines in our difficult contemporary world, but the Secretary General himself has been engaged in discussions on this subject with Canada and with other countries. While I cannot go farther at this time, I want the house to know that we continue to do all we can, together with the United States government, the British government, and other governments in seeing that every effort is made to bring about negotiations in this very difficult situation.
Many other questions have been asked during the course of this debate and it would be impossible to deal with them all. When the External Affairs Committee meets we shall have an opportunity of considering these questions. In addition, when the estimates for the next fiscal year are before the house we shall have an opportunity of dealing in some detail with some of the matters that have been raised.
I think the house has been engaged in the past few days in a very vital discussion of 23033-57
Supply-External Affairs matters that are of the greatest moment not only to our own country and not only to the United Nations but also to the peace of the world. While the solution for these problems does not rest with one country, there nevertheless is an obligation on the part of all countries to do their utmost to try to minimize the sources of danger and the danger itself.
I have been in this house many years, Mr. Chairman, and I have not for a long time been moved as I was last night when I listened to the hon. lady, the member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I well remember her father sitting near where the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is now sitting. I could not help but detect the same constancy and strength of purpose in her plea for peace that we knew him to espouse when he was a distinguished member of this house.
I wish to assure the hon. lady that the government of Canada looks upon the United Nations as one of the cornerstones of our foreign policy. It is not our fault if collective security has not been fully secured in the United Nations during recent years. As the hon. lady knows, we have participated in every one of the peace keeping operations of the United Nations. We shall continue such participation because it forms part of a process which could assist in establishing a United Nations peace force.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
However, the hon. lady should not overlook the fact that Canada has made these endeavours in the face of great frustrations. A conference was held in Ottawa on these subjects which was designed to encourage action by those countries with peace keeping experience. We have repeatedly urged the members of the United Nations to assume collective responsibility for the financial burden imposed on the United Nations as a result of these peace keeping operations. We have not been able to get the kind of support on a sufficiently wide scale and from enough countries to make this possible, but she may be assured that just as we took the initiative in the establishment of a peace force on Cyprus, backed up by this parliament, we shall not hesitate to take a similar initiative in situations where we are able to do so in conjunction with the other members of the United Nations.

The foreign minister of Turkey said:
The question of Cyprus seemingly is leading Turkey to a war at a moment it does not wish, and in spite of Turkey's wanting peace.

The statement made the other day in the name of the governments of Greece and Cyprus-I am not now saying that there was an official statement but I have seen the report and I have my reason for putting it that way-attributing to both governments an agreement that the solution of the problem was enosis was objected to strongly by the government of Turkey. the second reading of Bill No. C-lll, to incorporate Bank of Western Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-lll is identical to one which was introduced in this house last year and which received second reading but did not receive final reading because of the dissolution of parliament.
The report of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance tabled last year recommends a more open and competitive banking system in Canada. It is the belief of the incorporators of the Bank of Western Canada that the creation of a new bank in western Canada with head office in Winnipeg, Manitoba, will meet some of the problems referred to in the report of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance, particularly the dangers of undue concentration in the banking and financial system of this country.
I should like to give a few basic reasons why this bank should be incorporated. First, the growth of Canada and particularly western Canada requires an increase in the banking institutions available to serve the economy. In 1954 Canada had ten chartered banks. Today it has only eight. The gross national product of Canada has doubled in
23033-57J

those ten years. Western Canada should have a bank with its head office, seat of control and management in western Canada. Only in this way will the financial needs of western Canada receive the close attention and understanding that they deserve.
The economy of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia is sufficiently varied and broadly based to support a western Canadian bank without recourse to the capital markets of Toronto, Montreal or New York. The capital needs for western provinces are sufficiently important to the people living there to warrant their asking parliament to incorporate a bank specially devoted to their needs.
Modest branches, economical and efficient service and concentration on small and medium sized accounts will be the keynote of the service to be provided by the Bank of Western Canada. There will be no need to support eastern head offices. The Bank of Western Canada will operate in a much more modest style than some of its eastern competitors.
The former minister of finance told the House of Commons last year that the government was not opposed to further competition in the banking field provided the three following conditions were met: (1) the new bank must be adequately financed; (2) it must be supported by financially responsible people; (3) provision should be made for retaining control in Canada. The Bank of Western Canada meets all three conditions.
The Bank of Western Canada would fill a growing need for a regional financial institution to take care of a regional economic development. Interprovincial co-operation between the four western provinces in the development of water resources, power, irrigation and mineral development point to the need for a financial institution based in the west and geared to the business opportunities that are developing in the west.
As to the bank, its head office will be at the city of Winnipeg in the province of Manitoba. All its directors will be subjects of Her Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada. If the bill is approved the special act incorporating the Bank of Western Canada will provide restrictions on the transfer of shares to nonresidents and a prohibition against ownership of the shares in this bank by non-residents exceeding 10 per cent of the total number of shares issued and outstanding.
The capital stock of the bank will be $25 million divided into 2,500,000 shares of $10

In addition to the initial subscribers of stock listed as incorporators in Bill C-lll there are now some 6,000 Canadian residents holding trustee subscription certificates entitling them to subscribe for stock in the new bank if and when incorporated by parliament. These trustee certificates would entitle these Canadian residents to subscribe for more than $6-i million of par value of stock in the new bank. In addition, more than 4,000 individual Canadian residents hold through investment companies certificates entitling them to subscribe for over $3 million par value of stock in the bank.
I consider that the proposal to incorporate the Bank of Western Canada should not be delayed because of any suggestion that parliament should await the passage of a revised Bank Act so as to know what conditions parliament might impose on banks in the future. All existing banks will be subject to the Bank Act as and when it is passed by parliament.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
Bill C-lll complies with the Bank Act as it now stands. The Bank Act and the Porter Commission report contemplate continuous competition and continuous expansion of the banking system in Canada to meet the growing economy of the country. I respectfully urge members of the house to allow this bill to go before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs where all questions arising in connection with it can be answered by interested and qualified parties.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say two or three things about the measure before us, Bill C-lll, an act to incorporate the Bank of Western Canada.
As the previous speaker has said, a similar application was made to the previous parliament. In my opinion both the bill and the application have considerable merit. If one reviews the history of banking in Canada one thing becomes apparent very early. When the western provinces entered confederation they found at least one arrangement which was securely established, namely, the banks in eastern and central Canada. Private banks such as the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Bank of Montreal and the Bank of Toronto were already in existence. I am not speaking for or against these institutions but I should like to draw attention to the fact that if we examine the national economy today we find it is
[Mr. Klchard.l
almost entirely different from what it was then, at the time the banking situation began to "gel". Everything else has changed in this country but we persist in going about many of our tasks and grappling with many of our problems as though nothing had altered.
Certainly the banking structure should be changed. I think it would be a healthy thing if we were to establish in this country a Bank of Western Canada in addition to the two or three large, very rich and very old banking institutions in the central and eastern parts of our country. I think it would be most sensible if there were in the western part of our country a bank especially established there to do business among, with and for the people and institutions of that area, separate and independent from the older banks in other parts of the country.
On the other hand, I must say I would be hesitant about urging approval at the present time of the bill now before us. As hon. members well recall, there was before the last parliament an application of a similar kind from the Bank of Western Canada. There was an application for a charter from the proposed Laurentide Bank and a third application for a charter to operate a bank in western Canada from the proposed Bank of British Columbia. As we all know, the applications of the first two banks, the Bank of Western Canada and the Laurentide Bank, were approved by the other place but the application of the Bank of British Columbia was not approved at that time.
I thought that in fairness to all the banks concerned, particularly the Bank of British Columbia, we should seek to make a decision on the application of all three banks at about the same time so that no one bank would have an advantage over the others.
The Bank of Western Canada has renewed its application for a charter and so has the Bank of British Columbia. I still support in principle the idea of the establishment of a Bank of Western Canada as outlined in the bill before us, but my point of view is that we should not tonight approve the sending forward of this application, at least until there has been time for the Bank of British Columbia application to go forward in the other place where it is now, one might say, on the rails.
Having said that, I will conclude my remarks on this subject. I favour the establishment of this new bank but I would urge that we do not move on with it until there has
February 8, 1966

been a proper opportunity for the other applications to be heard.

Mr. Speaker, I am interested in seeing that Bill C-lll is approved in principle so that it may be presented at the proper moment before the Committee on Banking and Commerce. It seems to me that regardless of what we may think about the application of the Bank of British Columbia, which we expect will be forthcoming, we should be consistent when it comes to giving approval in principle to the legislation before us.
I was interested in what the hon. member who introduced the bill had to say about the reduction in the number of banks operating in Canada today. I am wondering whether, after all our work to get new banks established in western Canada, we may not be faced one day by pressure from the larger banks of central Canada to absorb these smaller and more recent institutions. Of course, we shall have to take this into consideration when the Banking and Commerce Committee opens its study of the matter. I merely express the hope that those who support the application of the Bank of Western Canada will give their support equally to the applications of the Laurentide Bank and the Bank of British Columbia if such applications come before us so that we may be consistent in our approach to this whole banking question.
There is something else which I believe we should take into consideration and this too should be discussed in the banking and commerce committee. I refer to the fiscal policy of the government as it relates to those areas in Canada where there is a possibility of inflation and to those other areas where there is a need for credit. These two contrasting situations can exist in Canada at the same time. At the present time we find a blanket policy being applied by the Bank of Canada. Whenever an inflationary trend exists a tight money policy is introduced; yet this policy adversely affects areas where credit is really needed, causing concern and hardship in those areas. It is my view that we must build into our banking policy a flexibility which will enable us to take care of these inflationary tendencies without unduly hampering those areas where expanded credit is required.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
There seems to be a paradox here. When we talk about the balance of payments between Canada and the country to the south we
Private Bills
seem to feel that certain restrictions must be imposed. This may be so but in connection with our fiscal policy I believe the following to be true. We must take into consideration the fact that our policies extend chiefly to areas in which our primary producers operate. These are the people who are our greatest exporters, and the availability of credit under a tight money policy which affects the progress of our primary producers also affects our exports to the United States and as a consequence our balance of payments problem. We need to take a very close look at this particular aspect of the banking situation in Canada.
Another thing we must examine in connection with Canadian banks is their share setup. All too often we hear the claim that it does not matter how much money Canadian banks make, how much they take in, or how much the national debt is because it will be returned to the people in the form of dividends. But this is only true if bank shares are owned by Canadian citizens. When we deal with banking applications in the Banking and Commerce Committee we must give serious consideration to this aspect.
One more thing I should like to mention is the revision of the Bank Act, and at the outset I wish to say that I think in Canada we have the greatest banking system in the world. I believe there is no better banking system anywhere but there are some shortcomings which have allowed the outside world's financial system to draw off great volumes of credit from Canada in the way of dividends for monetizing prospectuses. In other words, a foreign bank can monetize a prospectus-I am thinking now of situations where we have raw materials in abundance- but under the law a Canadian bank cannot monetize it. We shall have to give consideration to that aspect of banking when we are discussing the Bank Act and the position of chartered banks in Canada.
It is ridiculous that I for one or any other person may have in my possession a great deal of raw material alienated from the crown through a lease or by some other method but do not have sufficient money to move in and provide the capital equipment and plant necessary to develop the natural resource involved and convert it into a finished product. We cannot do this in Canada but United States banks, the Netherlands Bank or Barclays Bank can come along and use a Canadian asset and thereby

Having done so they reap the benefit of the great interest rate that they charge on the money thus provided. I say it is time Canadian banks were given this right so that we can get to the point where we can develop our own resources for our own benefit and not for the interest bearing benefit of foreign banks. I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying we are in favour of this bill in principle and will vote for its passage.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Did he use the expression "monetize a prospectus" and, if so, What does he mean?

To give an example, I have been in the lumber business so I orient myself to the trees. I was able to get a pulp harvesting licence by virtue of credit which I was able to raise myself and through my colleagues, but I was unable to get the type of money I needed for the development of that pulp harvesting area. I cannot, by taking a good prospectus to a proper bank, get money to develop that pulp harvesting area. The banks today cannot take security on fixed assets leading to capital account in this way, and it is time we looked at our banking institutions and saw to it that in at least some degree they are given the opportunity to advance credit with security on fixed assets.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this bill I would first like to make it clear that I am speaking in my capacity as a private member and, second, that I have no particular brief for the Bank of Western Canada.
I should like to see more banks in this country. Certainly I should like to see greater competition among our banking and other monetary institutions, and most definitely I should like to see banks which are more responsive to the needs of particular areas of the country, especially to the western parts of the country. In preamble, however, I should also like to make it quite clear that I believe

the nation must remain in charge of our monetary affairs.
There are various headings under which the nation must remain pre-eminent. These are external affairs, defence, external trade, immigration and, most emphatically, money and banking. It is essential that our financial institutions operate under a set of rules or laws which are national in scope.
It is only by operating under this broad umbrella, and I suggest a single umbrella, that we will have the monetary flexibility necessary to develop this large country, a country which is going to grow northward and westward with the passage of time.
Reference has been made to banks which might be incorporated both privately and by the provinces. I should like to make it quite clear that I believe we can have one publicly owned bank in this country, the Bank of Canada. It already exists. It is the central bank of the nation. Personally I should not like to see our provinces in a position of ownership, in other words, in a position of control of major banks, and by that I mean the chartered banks.

Later on it makes it quite clear that these matters are not ones which are subject to the jurisdiction of the provinces.
Last year the former minister of finance spoke on this subject and I trust his remarks will be endorsed by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). He underlined that the B.N.A. Act clearly assigns to this parliament exclusive jurisdiction over banking and the incorporation of banks, and he went on to say:
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
Even a limited ownership of shares of a bank by another government, whether it be a foreign government or a provincial government, could place such a government in a special position of power or influence in relation to that bank.
February 8, 1966

And further:
Such a situation might lead to differences of opinion between the government and another government, and to confusion over who exercises authority in regard to the bank. In order to avoid this danger the proposed amendments will provide that no shares of a chartered or savings bank may be registered in the name of any government or its agents.
I suggest that this is crucial and that this authority must be clearly identified. It must be clearly identified as the national authority.
The principal argument used by the province of British Columbia last year is that provinces have control over property and civil rights, that shares in any enterprise are property and hence a province can have control over bank shares and can properly buy a controlling interest in a bank. I suggest that many of the operations of such a bank, at least as it was proposed last year, would extend beyond the borders of British Columbia and therefore would certainly go into areas and territories which were not solely under the jurisdiction of the province.
I should like again to emphasize the need for more banks. I have stressed the need for more privately owned banks which are totally responsive to the laws of Canada and subject to the monetary and fiscal laws of this country. As other members have indicated, there have been more banks in Canada's history. I believe in the 1880's there were as many as 40 in number. This number has now dwindled to eight. We need more banks, as I have suggested, banks which are more sensitive to the needs of western Canada.
Western Canada is extremely prosperous. If you take the Manitoba-Ontario boundary as the dividing line, western Canada contains certainly more geography, more territory, than all the rest of Canada combined. It also has a population comparable with that of the province of Quebec. It generates wealth comparable already with that of the province of Ontario. It is of considerable consequence, witness the fact that it generates high incomes and high savings.
The second annual review of the Economic Council of Canada, its latest report, at page 101 indicates that the levels of personal income in all the provinces of western Canada are well above the national average. The national average is approximately $1,500 per year. In British Columbia the average income is more than $2,000 per year; in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba it is $1,750, all obviously well above the national average of $1,500.
Private Bills
On turning to pages 120 and 121 of that annual review we see tables which rank our western provinces as first, second, third and fifth in respect of, (a), annual investment per capita and, (b), capital stock of machinery and equipment per person in this country. In other words, our western provinces are right at the top not only in so far as incomes and savings are concerned but also in respect of the need for new capital, the need for more funds and the need for additional banking facilities.
I should now like to say a word about the scale and the size of this proposed Bank of Western Canada. I notice its authorized capital is set out at $25 million. This is a sizeable bank. However, several of the banks in eastern Canada are larger. The Toronto-Dominion Bank, for example, is approximately five times this size.
I should like to throw into perspective last year's application by the Bank of British Columbia, the B.C. government sponsored bank. It had a proposed authorized capital of $100 million, in other words, four times the size of the proposed Bank of Western Canada. That particular bank, if it were to be operated as are other chartered banks, making a reasonable profit or return on equity capital, would have had to commandeer all of the savings, public, private, industrial and personal, in the province of British Columbia in order to make a go of things. That was to be an immense undertaking. Perhaps western Canada could sustain a bank or banks of that size in years to come. I am all in support of a Bank of British Columbia if it is a private bank. I am for such a Bank of British Columbia even though the initiative came or may come from the premier of the province of British Columbia. My only concern is that the controlling shares will not be held by a provincial government, including the present provincial government of the province of British Columbia.
Why?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
If this bank of the province of British Columbia could be sponsored and thrive as the result of the initiative taken by the premier of the province of British Columbia that would be fine, but it must be a private bank totally responsive to the laws of the nation so that our national banking system can continue to survive. I would hate to think that we would have 10 separate provincial banks, each of which dominated all the financial activities of its particular province. There

February 8, 1968
Private Bills
would be little room left for the Bank of Canada.
I wonder if the hon. member would answer a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I should be glad to in a moment but I want to finish my thought.
This is the time I want to ask a question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Would the hon. member wait a moment? Imagine ten different provincially owned banking systems, and this is not stretching the concept too far. Not only has the province of British Columbia shown a definite and tangible interest in this field but Hon. Eric Kierans has made comments in this direction in respect of Quebec. I can therefore visualize a bank of Quebec being incorporated the moment a bank of British Columbia owned and controlled by the province of B.C., was set up.
Why not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
I believe a member of the N.D.P. asked "why not?". This is certainly stretching one's imagination a great deal but I would ask him to visualize his leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) as prime minister of this country trying to determine monetary policy in circumstances where his influence was limited to the Bank of Canada. He would have to negotiate with the ten provincial premiers. If he had to do that today he would be sitting down with ten premiers who are certainly not members of the New Democratic party. He would have a great deal of difficulty in developing monetary policy which was consistent with his own ideas of how things should run.
Under such circumstances the Prime Minister would be in great difficulty. There would be a certain amount of horse trading going on at these federal-provincial conferences. I can imagine the province of British Columbia saying, for instance, we will go part way on a tight money policy if you will turn over your offshore mineral rights to the province of British Columbia. That is the sort of thing that could happen. One might call them political considerations or say that they were considerations extraneous to money and banking, but they would be injected into these federal-provincial conferences with the result that you would not have a really effective, non-partisan, non-political banking system in this country. I want to see one

system, not ten different systems or eleven competing systems if you permit the national government to remain in the field.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
There have been experiences elsewhere in this regard. The N.D.P. members have suggested there should be provincially owned banks. I notice that in the United Kingdom the Labour government has not sought to nationalize any of the chartered banks. It has used the central bank, the Bank of England, as the principal authority through which it can carry out its banking and monetary policies. It has used the leverage which that central bank has on the commercial banks in order to put its policies into effect. In the United Kingdom there has been no problem of divided jurisdictions, of regional banks, certainly not regional banks which were autonomous in their field.
I suggest we would do well to note what the Labour party has done in the United Kingdom in this connection. Members of the New Democratic party in this house indeed might care to comment on the success the Labour party has achieved with one central bank, that is, one nationally-owned bank and no other government-owned banks.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about another matter which the Porter Royal Commission raised with respect to banking and finance. I refer to the limitations placed on our chartered banks in respect of, first, the interest rate ceiling and, second, the funds which they have to deposit with the central bank, the Bank of Canada, measures which from a financial point of view present a limitation on their activities.
I have not made up my mind whether I should like to see the interest ceiling removed. I am inclined to say that I should like it removed if only because it would generate greater competition among the chartered banks, the trust and loan companies, etc. I should like to point out that our chartered banks have not been growing as rapidly as other institutions in the monetary field. In other words, our chartered bank business, to which the Bank of Western Canada should be admitted, has not grown as quickly as has the business of the mortgage, loan and trust companies, caisses populaires and credit unions.
Indeed, in scanning through the report of the Porter Royal Commission I find that chartered bank deposits since 1945, that is, in the post-war period, have a little more than doubled. The mortgage and loan companies'
February 8, 1966

assets have risen more than sixfold. The trust companies' assets have gone up about seven times. The caisses populaires' and credit unions' assets have risen more than fifteenfold. In other words, these other major categories of financial activity have grown faster, I suggest very much faster, than the business of the chartered banks.
Therefore the Bank of Western Canada is entering a field but it is a limited one, a field with certain requirements, stipulations and limitations. It is entering a field which is clearly subject to federal jurisdiction but a field that is not growing as rapidly as the other financial institutions and lines of financial activity in this country.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to see some of the dividing lines between the different categories of financial activity removed. I should like to see greater competition between these different financial institutions, and I should certainly like to see them more responsive to the needs of different parts of the country. This will come about, I trust, as a result of the incorporation of more banks like the Bank of Western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we are debating the second reading of this bill for a third time. It was perhaps a tragedy for those people who support the incorporation of the Bank of Western Canada that this bill too was a victim of the premature election called last August, because the Committee on Banking and Commerce had given its sponsors an undertaking that it would be dealt with in committee last September. Notices were actually published so that interested parties could prepare briefs and in order that public representations could be made with regard to this and other banks the incorporation of which was being sponsored by private members. But all this was washed down the drain by that rather quixotic act of the government in calling an election.
However, be that as it may; there is no point in crying over spilled milk. I believe we must show some consideration for those people who have invested their money in this commercial proposition. They are entitled to the same consideration as anyone else. They have the complete right to be heard and heard promptly. It behooves us to get on with the second reading of this bill and send it to the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs because I believe the house has now reached the point where it believes that matters of this kind are better discussed in
Private Bills
committee where we can hear public representations and question witnesses.
There are many questions we shall ask on this matter. I do not wish to prejudge the yeas or the nays in respect of this bank. I find that its name is rather euphemistic because its control remains in central or eastern Canada. It has for its own purposes enlisted the support of many people in the prairie provinces but their participation is technically nominal.
We want to know why there is this attraction to the eminent gentlemen from Toronto and so forth in the name Bank of "Western" Canada. Whether it is a sop to their conscience for past conduct I do not know. In any event it is one of the matters we should like to examine when this bill is brought before the committee.
As one of the members of the committee I shall limit my discussion on the principle of the incorporation of the Bank of Western Canada to these few words and hope we shall discuss it before the committee in the very near future.

Mr. Speaker, speaking at the same level as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis), since he demoted himself for the time being from his role as parliamentary secretary I believe one or two comments are necessary with respect to his remarks. On balance I suggest his was a most interesting speech, well documented and well larded with references and statistics. It was perhaps more appropriate in a debate on the Throne Speech or on the Bank Act than on the bill before us because the hon. member ranged rather far afield in his implications.
I do not wish to transgress the rules of the house and hope I shall not be called to order if I make reference to some of the points mentioned by the hon. member. He referred to the question of competition and his desire, as I gathered, to see a greater degree of competition in the banking industry. He coupled with that the suggestion, as I understood him, that if there was an increase in the interest rate permissible under the Bank Act this would beget an increased degree of competition.
I do not know whether at that point he was referring only to banks under the Bank Act or to the whole field of lending which includes trust, loan companies and the like. In any event, the concept of competition among banking institutions in this nation is a fallacious one and anyone who advocates the idea

February 8, 1966
Private Bills
that there will be more competition among banking institutions is advocating something that is incorrect in fact.
I say this because banks that are chartered under the Bank Act are controlled by a piece of legislation of this parliament and are not permitted to deviate. There is interest rate limit now and presumably there will be a limit later when the Bank Act is revised. Perhaps the limit will be higher on the interest rate which can be charged. Who knows? There is universal application of the interest payable on savings accounts and so on.
The only type of competition, as I have said before, that exists in the private chartered bank industry is competition in smiles on the part of managers and competition in the form of the fronts of the banks themselves, whether they consist to a greater or lesser extent of glass. The competition is in the form of architectural design, in the form of modern furniture, paintings and the like within banks, both main offices and branches, that have been built in recent years. But in terms of competition in the sense of dollars and cents from which the bank customer benefits there is no competition. I submit that any argument that there will be more competition does not refer to competition in a sense that means anything to the average customer of our banks.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
The hon. member also painted an extravagant picture of the situation which might prevail if provincial governments were permitted to invest in the shares of banks. He indicated that if such were the case there would be chaos in the nation. In fact, he said we would have ten or eleven banking institutions competing with each other and presumably the chartered banks which exist at the moment would be driven out of business if we follow his argument to its conclusion.
I submit that the falsity in that sort of reasoning is that the hon. member presumes there will be no authority or control in the hands of the Bank of Canada, that there will be no authority or control in the Bank Act regulating the operations of private chartered banks. He seems to presume that this control will be abdicated in favour of provincial governments if provincial governments are allowed to invest in the shares of banking institutions. This is just arrant nonsense. All the hon. member is trying to do is justify an anticipated announcement by the minister

when he introduces amendments to the Bank Act.
The hon. member is also trying to justify the position taken by the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), as well as the vested interest expressed by the members of the Senate when they turned down the application of the Bank of British Columbia. This was done for political reasons and because some senators had a vested interest in that they were directors or had invested in shares of chartered banks. They were acting from self-interest rather than in the interests of British Columbia. These are facts. We do not need the hon. member for Coast-Capilano or any other apologist for the government to tell us about this matter. The facts are there for everyone to see.
As a result of this action the economic development of British Columbia, to which the sponsor of this bill paid such glowing tribute, has been hindered. This selfish interference has been buttressed by an announcement from the former minister of finance. Presumably the way is now being paved by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano and others for pressing the Minister of Finance to introduce amendments to the Bank Act which would interfere with the jurisdictional authority of provincial governments under the British North America Act.
One of the interesting aspects of the hon. member's remarks was the tender approach he made to an increase in the interest rate. I do not know if this was a forewarning of things to come in the budget but if it is and if he has any intimate knowledge I think it was incorrect for him to even leak the possibility that there might be an increase in the interest rate of the private chartered banks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: That is my own personal opinion.

This is his personal opinion. However, it is the opinion also of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Louis Ras-minsky. Last night, speaking at Halifax to the Board of Trade, he also tenderly put out the thought that this would be good for the nation.
The Governor of the Bank of Canada left the impression that there should be an increase in the interest rate under the Bank Act. I presume Mr. Rasminsky is not expressing his own opinion. After all, he is the Governor of the Bank of Canada and there is a rapport between him and the cabinet. Since
February 8, 1966

the Coyne affair I have thought that when the Governor of the Bank of Canada spoke he spoke with the authority of the government behind him. Let me quote Mr. Rasminsky's words with respect to the question of interest rates:
The extent to which it is appropriate for the monetary authorities to permit credit conditions to tighten in any given circumstances must inevitably be a matter of judgment and I have been interested to note that in its submission to the Minister of Finance last week, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce expressed the view that in present circumstances it would be appropriate for Canada to pursue "a more vigorous monetary policy and impose more monetary discipline".
This is just one quotation from the remarks of Mr. Rasminsky in which he is presaging the budget and presaging the introduction of amendments to the Bank Act. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano, expressing his personal opinion as he just did, is also leading us in that direction.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: May I ask a question?
Gladly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys

Laurentide Bank on a retail-wholesale basis in dealing with money was being questioned, and I think properly so, in this chamber, and they did not want any closer public scrutiny of this relationship.
I think that the Laurentide Bank or Laurentide Finance Company is probably awaiting the introduction of the Bank Act revisions, hoping that they will reflect one of the provisions contained in the bill last year, namely, that in the future banks can be incorporated by letters patent. Then Laurentide Finance Company, with its connections with the Liberal party, will be able to apply for incorporation of the Laurentide Bank and become involved in the wholesale-retail process of dealing in money, and will not have to subject that relationship to public scrutiny in parliament. If that is the course on which they intend to embark, I suppose the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) will accommodate them when he brings in the revisions to the Bank Act, following the action of his predecessor last year, and will give them that opportunity to get in by the back door inasmuch as they are afraid of public scrutiny of their relationship and their structure.

I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member for Skeena in his interesting speech but I should like to place before Your Honour a point of order. In one sense I am rather pleased because I do have so much more to say about this bill, Mr. Speaker, which perhaps will have to wait for another time. Tomorrow is a rather important day in the life of the Bank of Western Canada and the Bank of British Columbia. Because we in the

New Democratic party believe in the principle of togetherness we think that the applications of both banks should proceed at relatively the same speed through parliament so that one will not have a leg up on the other when it comes to incorporation and getting down to business.
I understand that tomorrow it is hoped that the Bank of British Columbia bill will be introduced in the Senate for first reading. This will give us an opportunity to see what its proposed structure will be. We do have some friends in the Senate and we will be able to consult with some of our friends over there.
Who are they?
I am asked to name them but I do not want to embarrass the hon. gentleman.
I would not be embarrassed.

We will be able to assess whether or not the Bank of British Columbia bill will be given favourable treatment by the Senate. If it is, all well and good. The Bank of Western Canada legislation now before us will also be given favourable consideration. If there is the possibility of a hitch or hold-up or delay or defeat of the Bank of British Columbia bill in the Senate, then the same course of action will have to be followed here in the house and every means possible used to defeat the Bank of Western Canada legislation, because we believe in the principle of equality of treatment and no favouritism.

It is proper that this should be said because I will now give the minister a version that appeared today in a La Presse editorial signed by Guy Cormier.
