This afternoon the minister did answer quite a number of inquiries in this debate. Quite a few still remain, however, that he has not answered. I think that it would shorten this debate very considerably if the minister could give us more answers to the questions he is asked. There are quite a number of items outstanding that he has not mentioned as yet.
Will he provide to the members of the house a White Paper on the facts of the Rhodesian situation in general? As the minister indicated this afternoon, it was because of the internal situation in Rhodesia that Canada is participating in these sanctions. I think we all know, Mr. Chairman, that undoubtedly the real reason why this whole matter came before the United Nations, as a matter of great concern, was because of the pressure of peoples in the African countries and because of the treatment, or the alleged treatment-and we have not been able to find the exact facts as yet-of the very large majority of African citizens in Rhodesia.
At an early date will the minister undertake to provide the members of the house
February 8, 1966	COMMONS
with a White Paper dealing with the tacts? I realize that it will take a while to prepare, but it would answer some of the questions I brought up on several occasions during this debate.
The question is whether in fact it is true that the leader of the nationalist group in Rhodesia would expropriate all lands of Europeans without compensation. Is it true that the present leader in Southern Rhodesia, Mr. Smith, has indicated that he will not provide any kind of representation or vote for the African majority in the area? As I say, the minister partially replied to the question of what are the terms of the offer of Mr. Smith to the British government, and vice-versa. He has answered some of these things, but I think it would be much better if, in this case, there were produced a White Paper by the Department of External Affairs which could be made available to members of the house.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
This leads to the next question. What is going to happen if this house is not in session and it turns out that economic sanctions are not entirely satisfactory or do not achieve the desired effect. What does the government intend to do then? Will it go further? I still maintain, for this party, that the actions taken by the government were illegal. In support, the hon. member for York South indicated that they were undertaken on a somewhat shaky legal basis. But should the government consider it necessary to go further, what legal authority would they have? I would like to point out, in answer to one of the questions asked, that the Smith government made its illegal declaration apparently because it had become clear, after lengthy negotiation during which, as is well known, successive British governments explored every possibility of compromise, that the British government was only prepared to grant independence on a basis which would assure the achievement of majority rule in a relatively short period rather than the very long, almost infinite period contemplated by Mr. Smith and his colleagues. The British had also insisted that any arrangements for independence would have to receive the consent of the people of Rhodesia as a whole.
As to the use of force, we believe that, in view of the dangerous situation which could evolve, this is something one should look at with the greatest care. Certainly, that would be the position of Canada. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre asked whether we would support the use of force, should sanctions fail. This was the question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre as well as by the hon. member for Oxford a few moments ago. Our view is that economic sanctions are greatly preferable to the use of force. We are doing our best to see that these sanctions succeed. We think they will succeed. It is hard to see how the Smith regime can continue when its supporters must fully realize that their exports, imports and sources of finance have been cut off and will remain cut off. The British have not precluded the use of force in order to restore law and order in Rhodesia, according to declarations made by the British government. This was made clear in the communique following the Prime Ministers' Conference in Lagos. It is also a fact that the British government has declared itself unwilling to use force in existing circumstances. Canada agrees with this position. The matter is, of course, in this regard entirely one within the responsibility of the government of Britain.

Mr. Chairman, when the NATO review is over it will be possible to give a more definite reply with regard to the last question.
With regard to the question that agitated my hon. friend from Oxford, it was a United Nations resolution which provided in effect that arms were not to be shipped to Portugal. Canada respected this to the point that it has been the policy of the Canadian government since 1960 not to permit the export to Portugal, and territories under Portuguese administration, of any arms and equipment which in our opinion could be used for

military purposes in the Portuguese overseas territories.
With respect to the allegations of the hon. member for Kootenay West, to my knowledge there has been no secrecy about the cold weather trials. As far back as August 12 of last year the Department of National Defence issued a press release announcing that cold weather trials of German armoured vehicles would be conducted this winter at Camp Shilo by a team of approximately 100 German army and civilian experts. The press release gave details of the equipment to be tested and explained that the purpose of the trials was to determine the operational capabilities of the equipment, in accordance with NATO standards under low temperature conditions.
To show how little secrecy was involved, later a press conference concerning the trials was held at Camp Shilo-
On what date?

On December 16, which was approximately two weeks after the main body of German personnel arrived there. Also, on December 22, while I was away from Ottawa, an official of my department elaborated further on the purpose and nature of the trials at Camp Shilo. This is the spokesman, I suppose, to which my hon. friend refers.
Who was the spokesman?

I do not know. It was the official in the department who had that responsibility.
The use of the military facilities of one NATO country for equipment trials and training of forces of another is an established form of co-operation between NATO partners, and the Canadian government considers such co-operation with its NATO allies to be an integral and important feature of our general defence effort. Under the NATO air crew training program, for example, some 6,000 personnel from a number of countries including the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany, Belgium and Luxembourg have been trained in Canada. Just recently a group of U.S. marines completed cold weather training at Camp Gagetown.
When my hon. friend asked this question some days ago I said I perfectly understood the feelings of some persons in Canada regarding this matter and we took this into account, but we also took into account the fact that we have obligations to a NATO partner and we do not apologize for having taken this particular course.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to pursue the line of questioning that has been followed by my hon. friend from Kootenay West even though the troops under discussion tonight happen to be located within hailing distance of my native city of Brandon, Manitoba. It was interesting to note when the troops first arrived in that area, there was quite a flurry of interest in the local press as well as in the Winnipeg press, with letters to the editors pro and con the wisdom of bringing representatives of the German army to train in Canada.
I can tell the hon. member for Kootenay West that so far as the weather was concerned Manitoba gave these troops a very cold reception, with the prevailing temperature being down around 40 and 50 degrees below zero most of the training period. But on the other hand the citizens of the city of Brandon gave them a very warm and cordial reception.
It has been interesting to note that various groups within the city, including church groups, have been extending hospitality, largely because under the NATO program there are some 28,000 Canadians located in the city of Soest.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
No one who has visited that community would come to any other conclusion than I did, that it looks like a little bit of Canada located in West Germany. I may also say that during the previous winter elements of the British army were located at Camp Shilo undergoing the same type of training. They also had a very cold reception as far as weather is concerned, but at the same time they received a very warm response and were extended the hospitality of the good citizens of the city of Brandon. At the commencement of my remarks I stated that I was


not going to pursue this subject other than to indicate that this is a reciprocal arrangement we have accepted under our obligations as a member of the NATO alliance.
In my comments I wish to give the minister an opportunity to accentuate the positive. The discussion to the present time has placed him in a position where he has had to take a negative attitude. He has been chastised for bypassing parliament with respect to the actions of the government relating to Rhodesia. There has also been some criticism that the minister has been a little too closely allied with the United States with respect to Viet Nam policies. In respect of the subject I wish to deal with briefly I suggest that the minister has not followed the United States example as closely as he might have, and I refer to the subject of foreign or external aid. I think he will agree that notwithstanding the faults of the government of the United States, their initiative and generosity in sponsoring the Marshall plan during the very critical period of post-war European development has been one of the great examples of unselfish and disinterested generosity on the part of a modern nation. I do not think it has any parallel in world history.
Canada has been following a far off policy, as it were, in respect of that example established by the United States government. I know the minister has this matter at heart, and that is why I am providing him with an opportunity to accentuate the positive. He has already made several speeches on this subject. I recall that just last June, for example, in a statement made in Toronto with respect to Canada's obligations in the field of foreign aid, he suggested that we should be contributing some $400 million, which is about twice the amount that was being expended by Canada in respect of all the various programs that had been launched up to that time. I can assist him in being positive because the gentleman who now holds the responsibility for the exchequer, the man who has the keys to the treasury-the new Minister of Finance-thinks precisely along the same lines as the Secretary of State for External Affairs in regard to this matter.
At a conference held in Toronto in 1961, known as the conference of the Canadian National Committee on UNESCO the present Minister of Finance made the following statement:
There is one good and sufficient reason for international aid, and that is that there are less fortunate people in the world who need our help. If they are grateful for our help so much the better.

If by reason of the aid they receive they become bigger customers for Canadian goods and services, better still. If our aid helps them to achieve what Professor W. W. Rostov calls "take off'' to set their feet firmly on the road to higher standards of living, without resort to communist dictatorships, the benefits to us are beyond measure. But the inspiration must be essentially humanitarian and unselfish. If it is not, if the primary purpose of our aid is to help ourselves rather than to help others we shall probably receive in return what we deserve and a good deal less than we expect.
That is part of the speech made by the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Eglinton. In the light of that statement I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs will receive the warm support of the Minister of Finance in respect of his statement that Canada's commitments could be readily increased from the present $200 million to $400 million. As I say, Canada has been following far off in its policy in this respect.
In 1960, as I recall it, we had a conference on this subject. Shortly after that conference the external aid office was established in the Department of External Affairs. For a short period of time there was rapid expansion in the number of programs in which Canada participated. Most of them are well known to members, but perhaps I can just refresh their memories by referring to the special fund that was established in 1959. Then there was the original program, to which Canada contributed a substantial amount-the Colombo plan.
The special fund came into effect in 1959; the Canada-West Indies program came into effect in 1958.
The special fund was another program altogether, and our pledge has been doubled.

That is the type of information we will be seeking in the minister's reply.
The Commonwealth fellowship and scholarship plan came into effect in 1960; the French speaking African education program came into effect in 1961; the special Commonwealth African aid program came into effect in 1960; the world bank program and the export financing program were launched in 1961; the world food program got under way in 1961 or 1962. This represents quite a large expansion in Canada's participation during those years following the establishment of the external aid office, and particularly after the conference held in 1960.

Mr. Chairman, I begin by expressing my disappointment in the attitude shown by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As he said this afternoon, this has been one of the best debates on external affairs in years; and that has been my experience in this house, which is not as extensive as that of the minister. However, since coming to the house I have always followed external affairs and without doubt there is a much greater interest shown in this subject than there used to be; more members participate, more members attend to listen to the debates.
During the last two or three days we have been dealing with matters of prime importance to Canada. The war in South Viet Nam, which is escalating and may eventually affect us very seriously, is a matter of the gravest importance to Canada. The events in Southern Rhodesia are of grave importance to the Commonwealth and again-who knows-perhaps to the peace of the world because if trouble breaks out there, we become involved.
There are other subjects, of course, in external affairs-it covers a very large field

Supply-External Affairs -but it so happens that on this occasion we have had these two major matters under discussion. I say to the minister that although he accuses me now and again, as he did the other evening, of being too belligerent-I am a man of peace, actually-we have conducted ourselves reasonably and sensibly during the course of what has been a serious debate.
Any participation on my part in the course of the last three days has been occasioned by a serious interest in the subject and based on a fair amount of research and study. Therefore I have not been putting idle questions to the minister; I have not tried to embarrass him. There have been some occasions when I have, but not during the course of this debate.
I have been trying seriously to obtain answers to questions which I think are important. I am sure other people consider them important, also. The minister has now reached that critical stage in the committee's consideration of his estimates where he is on the verge of losing the co-operative attitude of this side of the house.
During the years I have been all through the mill in this respect, sitting on that side of the chamber and this, and I know on what a narrow balance the passing of estimates hangs. I was government house leader for too long not to know the difficulty. Let me tell the minister, who has been here longer than I and should have learned more but has not, that he has now reached the stage where his estimates are not as likely to pass as they were just a few hours ago.
I will tell the minister why I say this. Instead of accepting our serious questions in the way in which they were put forward and giving us serious answers, the minister has adopted some of that arrogance of old, and carelessness. I was thinking just before the supper hour that dealing with the Secretary of State for External Affairs is like nailing jelly to the wall.
Picking up mercury with a fork.

You make an effort, and nothing happens. Let me show you, Mr. Chairman, how this arrogance appeared just this afternoon. This is what the minister said about that trade commissioner, "I am sure that the course we have taken is the correct

I hope he is not indirectly insulting our trade commissioner and the assistant trade commissioner who were there in the past. Were they not able men? Where is the Minister of Trade and Commerce to defend them? I interrupted the minister and asked, "How do you do that?" speechtext: What is that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I dealt with this and I took great pains to do so when I was replying to the hon. member for Oxford. I said we believe that economic sanctions will work. The British government believes that
February 8, 1966

Supply-External Affairs they will work. The British government had been urged by some countries in Africa to use force at the outset as the only effective way of dealing with the situation. This was not the view of the British government, nor was it our view at that time, nor is it our view now.
There are before the Security Council now proposals which have not yet been disposed of. If these proposals are adopted they would involve mandatory action. Thus far UN action has been confined to recommending economic sanctions. If the United Nations decided on a United Nations peace keeping operation, all countries in the organization would have to consider their position. We believe the way to settle this problem is to do what the British government and other governments have done. My hon. friend, who is a serious student of these matters, knows that this is a potentially dangerous situation. None of us would want to say in this house at this time anything that would be misunderstood in Africa or elsewhere. It seems to me that the course of prudence for us in Canada is to recognize the limitations, in a situation like this, for the use of force.

The minister does not realize I am trying to assist him. I want the minister to say, as these other prime ministers have said, that Canada is opposed to the use of force if sanctions fail; but he will not say it. I want the word to go out from here, just as Sir Douglas Home suggested in the British house that word would go out from that parliament, that Britain was interested in conciliation and negotiation, not the use of force. This is the word I should like to see go from this House of Commons. However, I cannot get the minister to come around to that point of view.
With his diversionary tactics, he talked about the Security Council and the resolution before that council concerning the use of force in Rhodesia. He did not go on to say that Great Britain is a member of the Security Council and that the veto is applicable in that council. Could you expect that Great Britain, a member of the Security Council holding a veto power like the other nations, would agree to a Security Council resolution demanding the use of force against a colony of Great Britain that would be mandatory, as the minister has said?
Then, we were treated to more diversionary tactics. If the United Nations, not the Security Council but the United Nations, came to an agreement that force should be


used in Southern Rhodesia, then the minister was careful not to say this would be mandatory. He said the countries would have to take a look at it. It is not mandatory coming from the General Assembly of the United Nations, but would be mandatory coming from the Security Council. I do not know why he had to go into that. I understand what he is talking about and I am still trying to assist him. He has not clearly stated the case in so far as Canada is concerned, and I think that is regrettable. I do not know why he cannot state that case. I do not know why he has taken such a severe attitude with regard to Southern Rhodesia. I think that the conciliatory approach would be better under these circumstances.
It is no comfort to anybody here that an illegal government has been established in Southern Rhodesia. It is no comfort to anyone here that four million Africans in Southern Rhodesia are denied their political freedom. However, there is some mutual ground. I should like the minister to tell us, now that we are on that point, does he favour the suggestion of one man one vote, which is a proposition put forward by a great many of the African nations? Is the minister prepared to answer that question? Does he favour the step by step process whereby political freedom emerges along with greater training and more education in Southern Rhodesia?
These questions have been the dividing line between those who have been opposing each other on what should be done in Southern Rhodesia. Does he say one man one vote now, which would mean the withdrawal of the Ian Smith government, the withdrawal of control by Great Britain, immediate independence granted-and you may have the blood bath occurring that some people have talked about?
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
The alternative course is the course of steady progress toward the emancipation of those who have not political freedom in Southern Rhodesia. Where does the minister stand on that matter? What course of action does he suggest? In response to the speech I made last night I should have thought that surely the minister could say yes to some of my suggestions. He could say yes, the Canadian government, the Canadian people, want to see the end of an illegal government in Southern Rhodesia, but that they want to see a progression toward complete independence. They want to see complete political freedom in that country carried out in stages
February 8, 1966	COMMONS
which will be acceptable to the experience and educational advance of the native population.
Everything does not have to be done all at once, Mr. Chairman. There is surely some responsibility on our side toward the Europeans who are living in Southern Rhodesia. We are not going just to throw them to the wolves, no matter how concerned we may be with regard to the native population of Southern Rhodesia. I do not know why nowadays we are so keen for everything to be done hurriedly. Unless my memory is faltering, I think centuries elapsed before it was a case of one woman one vote in Canada. The women of this country may say that things were terrible before this happened, but the men may have a different opinion.
How many centuries elapsed in this country before the native population, dispossessed by the French and the English, were given the right to vote? How many centuries elapsed before a representative of the native races of this country had a place in the other chamber? Why the great haste regarding some of these other countries in the world? speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend and I obviously do not agree on this question of Rhodesia. We have had certain exchanges and I have stated the position of the government. I indicated that we were opposed to the unilateral declaration of independence; that we had stated so long before the event took place and that we were not alone, that this was a Commonwealth position. I also stated that the arrangements between the government of Rhodesia and the government of Britain were something which were the responsibility of those two governments alone. Commonwealth involvement arose because of this unilateral declaration of independence, which we said long before could not be accepted, and for a number of other reasons. First came its implications for Commonwealth unity; second, this step involved a form of discrimination which could not be accepted and was not being accepted by the great majority of the nations in the world.
As to the particular situation with respect to the treatment of blacks and the treatment of whites in that country, that is a matter which involves negotiations between the two entities, one of which is now illegal, and the other now the colonial power. If my hon. friend would look at the White Paper of

Supply-External Affairs September 21 he would find there the five principles laid down by the British government, with which I am sure he is familiar.
Yes, I am.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
These five criteria had to be observed before there could be any independence accorded by the colonial power, Britain, to Rhodesia. These five criteria have not been observed.
The consequence of this is the action that we and other countries have taken. When the government of Mr. Smith falls, the government of Britain alone will have to determine which is the authority which will evolve out of the present power of the colonial authority. Britain will have to determine what conditions it will lay down for the successor to the present illegal regime in terms of removing discriminations. But to ask us-I say this with great respect to my hon. friend-to say what conditions could now be accepted by the British government would be an intrusion in its affairs in a manner which that country quite properly would resent, and with reason.

I am sorry if I cannot satisfy my hon. friend with regard to what would happen in the event of sanctions not succeeding. I cannot go any further than I have already. We continue to take that view, and we are not alone in that. That was also the view of the British government.

The Lagos conference committee will decide, by another decision at the end of a particular period, whether there will be another conference at which the matter will be reviewed. In other words, is Canada bound to go to the bitter end until Britain lifts the sanctions? That is the question I want to ask.

So far as Canada is concerned, there is a committee on which Canada is represented. That committee is observing the development of the sanctions program. So far as countries not being in the Commonwealth, and thereby not being on the Commonwealth committee, I cannot speak for them. They have voluntarily imposed sanctions. I mention countries such as the United States, the Scandinavian countries, Japan and some others. In the light of time they will have to determine whether they wish to continue. I can say without hesitation that those countries that have imposed sanctions have done so because they believed that this was essential to try to bring about tranquility in that part of the world.

What I should like to know from the minister is whether Canada is bound until the bitter end to go along with this. Are we steering our own course, or do we go in the same direction as Britain? I know that the purpose of the conference was to inquire whether these sanctions are successful. There is only one answer to my question. To be successful, sanctions must strangle the country they are imposed against. If they are successful the government of that country might well be brought to its knees, and thereby be in a better position for reconciliation. This parliament may feel that reconciliation has reached a certain point where we might say yes, whereas Great Britain might say, "No, that is not far enough. We want the five points. immobility of these teams in Saigon is due to the fact that about seven months ago the North Viet Nam government instructed the commission that the five teams made up of six or seven persons operating in the north should come back to Hanoi to avoid any danger. We know perfectly well that there was no danger at that time; this was a device to cause the commission to be unable to discharge its role of assessment. My hon. friend is quite right; at the moment it would not be possible to put teams in certain sections of the north, but I can say that attempts are being made to put teams in certain areas of the south. I assure my hon. friend that if I thought there was any way in which we could reduce these expenditures and at the same time discharge our international responsibility, reductions would be carried out forthwith. The stimulation I have received this evening would certainly cause me to act with alacrity.

We know there is a police state in Rhodesia. We know there is an illegal regime there. The tragedy of Rhodesia is, surely, that there has not been any marching along. There has been no preparation for these four million people to take over their rightful place in Rhodesian affairs. And the government there, with its short history-it has only been there since 1923 or so-is still living in the days of Cecil Rhodes.
It disturbs me very much to hear this word battle over sanctions. Of course, we had to have sanctions. I, for one, hope these sanctions will mean that the illegal government will fall, and the sooner the better. I do not think anybody has to make an announcement now as to what the position would be if the sanctions do not work. On orders of the day today I asked the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys a question which is of very considerable local importance in the Kootenays, and which also has national significance, although Mr. Speaker did not quite see it in that light. My question was this: Has the minister received a brief and a petition from the Nelson Rod and Gun Club through the British Columbia Wildlife Federation requesting the government of Canada to establish a definite anti-pollution policy with reasonable haste? If so, would the minister inform the house of his response to this petition.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that I am not sure whether the petition has yet arrived. But I mention this particularly because these are groups of people who are attempting to do something for Canada itself. These groups are studying this question, and the brief I wish to quote from is the result of persons meeting together in local organizations and in some cases travelling hundreds of miles to draft and to adopt a resolution, and finally a petition, and forward them to the appropriate department in Canada.
I am always one who likes to support local initiative and co-operation on the part of organizations which are interested in public affairs, whether they deal with natural resources, human rights or any other aspects of our society.
I will not quote the entire brief, but I will read this one paragraph:
Vested interests are naturally prejudiced against any mandatory involvement in agreements to provide adequate means to destroy the harmful effects of residue from their manufactured products, claiming the cost of pollution control is prohibitive, notwithstanding the fact that modern, scientific methods of eliminating man-made pollution of water is available.
Piecemeal adoption of water pollution control, such as a river system which is populated by one hundred villages, towns, and cities as an example, out of which three or four have sewage control, does not under any guise compensate the expense ratepayers of the individual sewage control systems are burdened with and who, in all sincerity, demonstrate their willingness to purify the river's water. If the remaining agencies dump unnecessary effluent into the river or its tributaries their efforts remain fruitless.
This subject has been discussed by municipalities, rod and gun clubs and other organizations owing to pollution which is developing in the Kootenay and in the Columbia rivers, particularly in the lower regions before they enter the United States. As

a result of these discussions the following resolution was adopted:

Whereas discrimination exists in British Columbia: If an individual builds a dwelling, where a septic type tank for sewage is required, it is mandatory that a system approved by the Department of Public Health be installed. In most cases these systems are expensive yet a city of ten to twenty thousand people may unceremoniously dump its sewage into the same river. Ore reduction mills are required to employ a settling basin to prevent acids, poisons, and slime from entering a stream, yet smelters and pulp mills may indiscriminately dump their wastes directly into the same waterway.
This is what is happening in the Kootenay region.
And whereas The Nelson Rod and Gun Club is a segment of organized society dedicated to the conservation of fish and wildlife and comprised of municipal, provincial, and federal taxpayers. It is fully conversant with the necessities of an expanding economy and is in no way intending to obstruct industry's effort to this end. We offer assistance in attaining a multiple use of resources, a live and let live policy that can assure a better way of life for laymen, industry and government; and further, while we are particularly concerned with water conditions existing and escalating in British Columbia, we recognize that this province is only one segment of the Dominion of Canada, all provinces, islands, Yukon and Northwest Territories. These have equal responsibility in the elimination of water pollution. The government of Canada must now have the responsibility for the implementation of a definite anti-pollution policy, the cost of which to be amortized over the years by industry and citizens of the Dominion of Canada.
Then the brief goes on:
Therefore be it resolved: We, The Nelson Rod and Gun Club, through the B.C. Wildlife Federation, petition the Government of Canada requesting an indiscriminatory and definite anti-pollution policy with reasonable haste.

maintopic: WATER RESOURCES-REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF ANTI-POLLUTION POLICY
speechtext:
Unfortunately I have not yet received that brief. The authors may be preparing a French translation. I hope to receive it within the next few days. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member's speech, however brief is of equal value.
It is not easy to devise, as requested by the brief, an anti-pollution policy. Everybody agrees there is need for such a policy. But it is not easy to formulate one because, as the brief implies, jurisdiction in this field is divided among the three orders or levels of government in Canada-municipal, provincial
February 8, 1966

and federal. Much of the fight against pollution is conducted at the municipal level as many of the major offences occur at the municipal level. The provinces are also interested. They claim, and I think they are entitled to claim, jurisdiction over natural resources; it follows that they must also have jurisdiction over offences against the proper use of those resources.
The federal government has jurisdiction over certain aspects of natural resources; for example, the Department of Agriculture, and of Health and Welfare are involved. The Department of External Affairs through its jurisdiction over international rivers is also concerned. In the past the Department of Industry had some jurisdiction because Atomic Energy of Canada Limited fell under the jurisdiction of that department. This crown company has now been transferred to my responsibility. It could even be claimed that the Department of Transport has an interest in the war against pollution, by way of its authority over navigable waters.
Then, as I say, jurisdiction is divided. A few weeks ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) thought it was high time at least to bring under one roof the different aspects of federal jurisdiction in the area of natural resources and, consequently, of pollution. In my view this is one of the major reasons for the creation of the department that was given to me. I can only promise the hon. member that we will do our best and we will try to do it as rapidly as possible. We are going to try to co-ordinate the federal jurisdiction in the field of natural resources and, consequently, in the field of pollution of natural resources.
I may add that already an interdepartmental committee of officials on pollution has been created. I might also add that the resource ministers' conference has announced that a three-day meeting will be held in Montreal, in November 1966, when all types of pollution will be discussed. Officials and experts from all over Canada will meet on this occasion.

I am rising at this point because there are millions of dollars in real estate values involved in the questions I have been asking for the past year and a half. I regret to say that practically no action has been taken by the government or the cabinet on this matter. Fingers are going to be burned before this matter is finally settled according to the law of the land.
My question this afternoon was directed to the Minister of Public Works because in the Navigable Waters Protection Act, which I have in my hand, it is pointed out that any work which is not built or placed in accordance with plans approved in advance by the Minister of Public Works may be removed and destroyed by the minister, and the cost of materials incidental to the removal, destruction or disposition of the work, deducting therefrom any sum that may be realized by sale or otherwise, is recoverable with costs in the name of Her Majesty from the owner.
I have been asking questions of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) in regard to interpretations of certain sections of international agreements and federal laws that apply to this problem of the filling of water lots. I think that to use the term, that I have been given the run around, would be to use the best description possible of the answers I have been getting, despite the requests of thousands of taxpayers in the metropolitan Toronto area for information as to what is the legal right of a lot owner.
On February 1, a week ago today, I asked a question of the Minister of Justice and I was told in the course of his reply that the problem seems to be the concern of two groups of individual land developers. It is unfortunate that when a person takes a case in point to emphasize the entire problem extending from the mouth of the Humber river to Etobicoke creek he is told that it is only one case. When we referred to the Millgate development we took a case which applies to a score or more of developers who are filling in lake Ontario between the Humber river and Etobicoke creek.
If the cabinet must have the names of everyone who is filling in between the Humber river and Etobicoke creek before they take action, I will give them a list and the dates. But I am trying to pinpoint the matter on one specific case, which in this instance is Millgate Investments who are filling in opposite Long Branch. In the
February 8, 1966

Navigable Waters Protection Act the following is pointed out as being part of the interpretation of the act:
"work" includes any bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier or other structure, tunnel or pipe, or telegraph or power cable or wire and the approaches or other works necessary or appurtenant thereto, or any work, structure or device, whether similar in character to the foregoing or not, which may interfere with navigation.
In the general section of the act it says:
No work shall be built or placed In, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless
(a)	the site and plans thereof have been approved by the minister; and
(b)	the work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with the plans and the regulations.
A year ago I asked on what date these plans were approved and the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works rose in his place and advised me that no approval has ever been given by the Department of Public Works for the filling in of water lots between the mouth of the Humber river and Etobicoke creek, a distance of four miles. Yet there are a score of land developers who have been filling in the lake. I am using Millgate Investments as an example, but I could give 19 more names. For instance, there is the property behind the Chicken restaurant, the property behind the Rainbow hotel and the property to the immediate east of the boundary of the town of Mimico. If the minister wants more, I can give them.
Here we have a case where the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works last June said that no prior approval had been given for the filling in of the lake. I have in my hand a letter dated last January 21 from the Assistant District Engineer of the Department of Works in Toronto which told Millgate Investments to stop filling in because it was illegal. Very interestingly, Millgate Investments told the village council of Long Branch in the month of March that they had lost the letter and did not find it until March 4, by which time the filling they wanted to do was completed. Very nice.
When we asked the Assistant Engineer in Toronto why they did not check to find out whether the filling was still going on to March, despite the letter of January 21, we were told, "We have not the staff to check and see whether our instructions are being followed".
On February 1 last the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) gave me an interesting answer as follows:
In the case to which the hon. member refers there was no obstruction of navigation-

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
This property extends 440 feet out into lake Ontario and is 330 feet wide. The Department of Public Works has demanded that during navigation season they put up two flashing lights at the end of the fill. Why do they demand that during navigation season two flashing lights be placed at the end of the fill, if there is no obstruction to navigation? The action of the department contradicts the statements of the Minister of Justice a week ago.
All we are asking is that the Department of Public Works withhold any approval of this application for cribwork to be placed around this illegal fill until the estimates of that department come before us. Trying to discuss this matter in seven minutes is not only ridiculous but makes a joke of the law. I have here pictures taken by commercial photographers showing the fill standing 30 feet in the air above the level of lake Ontario, and out into lake Ontario 100 and 150 feet. Yet we are told that it does not interfere with navigation. The letter refers to "commercial navigation," but the law does not say which may interfere with "commercial navigation"; it says "which may interfere with navigation".
A certain member of this side of the house passed the interesting remark a year ago, when the question was before us for consideration, that they might as well say it does not interfere with aerial navigation. The law says "which may interfere with navigation", and we receive the answer that it does not interfere with commercial navigation. The land is worth $100,000 to $200,000 per acre.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question raised this afternoon was whether I would assure the house that no permit would be granted until the estimates of the department came before the house for consideration. The difficulty in giving any such assurance as requested is, as I believe the hon. member will appreciate, that no minister is able to control the disposal of estimates in this house. The government can propose them to the house, but I am afraid it is an old saying, that is all too true, that the opposition disposes of them. This is the reason for the answer being made in that form. I believe it to be an accurate answer to the question as posed.
However, the subject is a very important and difficult one. There has been a great deal

Supply-Items Passed
of correspondence with the department on the subject of Mitigate Investments, and the correspondence indicates what I believe to be the genuine concern of a large number of people about this process of filling in water-lots in lake Ontario, and then using the filled waterlots as building sites. The difficulty arises in this case as to the jurisdiction of the federal government, which appears to be limited under our legislation to the question of whether or not the filling interferes with navigation.
There are, of course, other provisions in the act as to what the department can do in the circumstances. As I have said, there is a great deal of correspondence and a great deal of discussion about this subject. The hon. member has made many very strong representations. Perhaps it is really not possible to attempt to discuss the problem in detail in the three minutes allotted to me at this time.
We have been very concerned about the subject and have been trying to get some workable solution that will permit us, within the federal jurisdiction, to do what is effective to prevent any abuse of the law and at the same time have the province co-ordinate its efforts toward doing what lies within its jurisdiction to prevent any action being taken that is unreasonable. I have been in correspondence with the provincial minister and have arranged meetings which have been going on at the official level between the departments, with a view to trying to reach a better, more workable procedure to prevent any of these practices that are asserted by the hon. member, and I believe by a large number of people, to be a wrong use of the procedures they can take within the law.
Admittedly, the jurisdiction question is not clear, and the legislative provisions for action that can be taken are not as satisfactory or as clear as I would wish them to be. Perhaps I should terminate my remarks at that point. There is a good deal more that could and should be said about the details of the particular case, but as I say I do not think that it is possible to deal with them in the three minutes allotted to me.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.45 p.m.
